title: Active management strengthens recovery in China's freshwater protected areas
content:
Freshwater protected areas may not achieve ecological recovery through protection alone. Combining fishing bans with targeted fish removals can strengthen multidimensional native-fish recovery, while adaptive management that considers functional guilds, invasion context and ecological responses can further improve restoration outcomes.


Abstract

Research Highlight article about: Liang, Z., Rypel, A. L., Liu, J., & Guo, C. (2026). Targeted fish removals enhance multidimensional native fish diversity within freshwater protected areas. Journal of Applied Ecology, 63, e70521, https://doi.org/10.1111/1365-2664.70521. Freshwater protected areas (FPAs) are increasingly used to safeguard biodiversity and ecosystem services, yet protection alone may not always deliver ecological recovery, particularly where non-native species also benefit from reduced fishing pressure. Liang et al. (2026) address this challenge by comparing Chinese lake FPAs managed with and without targeted fish removals (TFRs). Their results indicate that recovery is multidimensional: combining FPAs with TFRs can enhance native fish diversity across taxonomic and functional dimensions while strengthening top-down trophic regulation. Importantly, outcomes depend on which ecological guilds are targeted, highlighting the need for adaptive and functionally informed management rather than uniform removal strategies. Rather than treating protection as an endpoint, Liang et al. (2026) show that freshwater recovery may require protection to work hand in hand with active management.
